starmer-defence-spending-claim.headline: Starmer made misleading claim on defence spending, watchdog finds
starmer-defence-spending-claim.body_md:
The claim sounded generous even by the standards of election-year defence pledges: Britain, the prime minister told MPs in March, would spend "£270 billion more on defence than we would otherwise have done" over the course of this Parliament. It was repeated by government accounts, including the Wales Office, which posted on social media that ministers had "delivered a £270 billion increase in defence spending." Neither statement was true, the UK's statistics watchdog has now ruled — and the ruling lands on a prime minister who has already left office.

In a letter dated 5 August, Penny Young, interim chair of the UK Statistics Authority, told shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge that the £270 billion figure was "incorrect and misleading." The number, an Office for Statistics Regulation investigation found, was not an increase at all — it was the total Ministry of Defence budget projected across the whole 2025/26–2028/29 period, worth £272.2 billion. Presenting the entire departmental spending envelope as new money, the watchdog concluded, overstated what had actually changed. Full Fact's own analysis of the underlying budget lines found the real year-on-year increases were far smaller: £1.9 billion between 2024/25 and 2025/26, and a projected £3.3 billion the year after — a fraction of the headline sum. The government's actual commitment has been to raise defence spending to 2.5% of GDP by April 2027, rising to 2.6% under NATO's broader accounting.

Cartlidge, who filed the original complaint, said the finding exposed "Labour's lies" on defence funding. The Wales Office has since corrected its post to describe the £270 billion as investment "over this Parliament" rather than an increase, and the Ministry of Defence said its statisticians were now working with communications staff to ensure "precise and consistent language" in future.

## A verdict that outlives the prime minister who earned it

What makes the timing awkward is that the ruling arrives for a government that has already changed hands. Keir Starmer resigned as prime minister on 20 July, succeeded by Andy Burnham, and the £270 billion claim now reads as a parting mark against a premiership that is over. But the institutional thread runs straight through to the present cabinet: John Healey, defence secretary when the disputed figure was first defended in Parliament, is now Burnham's chancellor, tasked with closing a defence budget gap estimated near £5 billion ahead of the autumn Budget.

![Official portrait of Keir Starmer](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Official_portrait_of_Keir_Starmer_MP_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Official_portrait_of_Keir_Starmer_MP_%28cropped%29.jpg)

That continuity matters more to bond investors than the rebuke itself. Thirty-year gilt yields have already climbed to their highest since 1998 as markets weigh Burnham's appetite for fiscal flexibility, and a watchdog finding that a predecessor inflated defence numbers by nearly £267 billion is unlikely to reassure anyone doing sums on the public finances. The story is not that Starmer misspoke — politicians routinely round generously in the chamber. It is that the same spending categories, the same funding gap and largely the same personnel are now back in front of the OBR, whose autumn verdict on the Budget will be the next real test of whether Burnham's government can describe its own numbers more carefully than its predecessor did.

water-utility-cyberattacks.headline: Cyberattacks hit water utilities in seven US states, Iran suspected
water-utility-cyberattacks.body_md:
Since late July, someone has been breaking into the computers that run American water systems — not to steal anything, but to see what they could switch off.

Across at least seven states, hackers gained remote access to programmable logic controllers, the small industrial computers that open valves, run pumps and regulate chemical dosing at drinking-water and wastewater plants. More than 30 municipal systems in Minnesota were hit, including the utility serving Plymouth, a suburb of roughly 80,000 people outside Minneapolis. Michigan reported intrusions at nine more. By the time the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued a nationwide advisory on July 30, some reports of new incidents were arriving from as far afield as South Dakota and Georgia. No utility has reported water that was unsafe to drink — operators lost visibility and control of equipment, not the ability to treat water safely — but several were reduced to running plants by hand while engineers rebuilt locked-out systems from scratch.

![Water treatment infrastructure of the kind targeted in the campaign](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a9/Dalecarlia_Water_Treatment_Plant.jpg)

## How you break into a water plant

The method was not sophisticated, which is part of what alarmed federal investigators. CISA said it was tracking "a significant increase in cyber threat actors targeting programmable logic controllers" made by Rockwell Automation, Siemens and Schneider Electric — three of the biggest names in industrial automation — plus the cellular modems many utilities use to check on remote pump stations, a blind spot that rarely shows up in routine security scans. Former FBI agent Michael McAndrews described the technique bluntly: "The attackers will scan the internet, and they'll look for the signature of known devices. When they find one, they simply try the default password." Once inside, the intruders changed passwords and reassigned IP addresses to lock operators out, in some cases triggering pressure loss and localized flooding before staff regained control.

![A programmable logic controller of the kind exploited in the campaign](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/42/PLC_Control_Panel.png)

There is a precedent, and it points toward Tehran. In November 2023, an Iranian Revolutionary Guard-linked group calling itself CyberAv3ngers hijacked an Israeli-made Unitronics controller at a water authority in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, defacing its display with an anti-Israel message. The Treasury Department later sanctioned six Iranian officials over that intrusion. This summer's campaign is quieter — no defacements, no ransom demands, which several analysts read as a sign the goal was reconnaissance or pre-positioning rather than extortion — but U.S. intelligence agencies have told NBC News and the Washington Post they suspect the same state actor is behind it.

## Iran, or "gross incompetence"?

The FBI has not formally attributed the campaign, and the White House has muddied the politics further. At a Cabinet meeting, President Trump dismissed the Iran theory and instead blamed Minnesota's "gross incompetence," a swipe widely read as aimed at Gov. Tim Walz. Walz fired back on social media:

> "Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too. This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there's no plan to win a war with Iran."

The exchange lands amid an unresolved standoff over Iran's nuclear program and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, and it underscores an awkward reality: attributing a cyber intrusion with certainty takes weeks, but the political reaction takes hours.

## The bill nobody has agreed to pay

What makes this episode more than a security footnote is timing. A Government Accountability Office report published in May — two months before the attacks began — warned that the EPA lacks the legal authority to require cybersecurity risk assessments across most of the country's roughly 170,000 drinking-water and wastewater systems, leaving compliance largely voluntary. Congress has since been sitting on two levers utilities say they need: the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program, which funds smaller utilities' defenses and is authorized only through September 30, and CISA's authority under the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act, which lets the agency and private companies swap threat data and which expires the same month. A coalition of operational-technology security groups, backed by CISA and the FBI, is now pushing Congress to reauthorize both before the deadline rather than let a funding lapse coincide with an active foreign intrusion campaign.

Separately, new rules under the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act will soon require utilities to report major breaches to CISA within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 — a mandate this episode will likely be cited to justify, given how long some utilities took to realize their controllers had been compromised. For the industrial-automation vendors named in the CISA advisory — Rockwell, Siemens, Schneider Electric — the episode cuts two ways: their equipment is the attack surface, but retrofitting tens of thousands of small utilities with segmented networks and modern authentication is exactly the kind of spending cycle that follows a scare like this one. The global market for critical-infrastructure cybersecurity was already estimated near $56 billion in 2025 and growing steadily; a coordinated, attributed nation-state campaign against a sector that mostly still runs on default passwords tends to pull that growth curve forward rather than change its direction.

The FBI's attribution finding, whenever it lands, will settle the Trump-Walz argument but not the underlying problem. The nearer deadline is September 30, when the grant program and the information-sharing law both lapse unless Congress acts — a bureaucratic date that, this year, doubles as a test of whether Washington treats a foreign hand on the tap as an emergency or just another line item.

trump-birthright-citizenship-orders.headline: Trump signs narrower executive orders targeting birthright citizenship and 'birth tourism'
trump-birthright-citizenship-orders.body_md:
President Trump signed two executive orders on Thursday narrowing who qualifies for automatic American citizenship at birth — a far more modest attempt than the sweeping order the Supreme Court struck down five weeks earlier, and one built specifically to avoid the same fate.

The first order, titled "Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship," denies birthright citizenship to children born in the United States to parents who are designated foreign terrorists or "alien enemies," to foreign government employees covered by diplomatic immunity, and to parents involved in commercial or fraudulent birth-tourism schemes. The second, "Ending Birth Tourism," directs the State Department and Homeland Security to deny visas, block entry and remove foreign nationals found to be travelling to the US for the specific purpose of giving birth. Federal agencies have 30 days to issue implementing guidance, and are barred in the meantime from accepting state-issued documents to certify citizenship for children who fall into the excluded categories.

"They're buying their way in, and we're not going to let it happen," Trump said at the signing, calling the current system "a disgrace." Deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, standing beside him, described the targets as "alien enemies of the United States, members of foreign terrorist organizations and large categories of people who lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments," and declared birth tourism "hereby banned."

![The U.S. Supreme Court building, whose June ruling in Trump v. Barbara forced the administration back to the drawing board on birthright citizenship.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Panorama_of_United_States_Supreme_Court_Building_at_Dusk.jpg/1280px-Panorama_of_United_States_Supreme_Court_Building_at_Dusk.jpg)

## A retreat dressed as an advance

The contrast with Trump's first attempt is deliberate. The executive order he signed on his first day back in office, in January 2025, would have denied citizenship to any child born in the US to a parent who was undocumented or present only temporarily — sweeping in the American-born children of visa holders, students and guest workers alongside those of unauthorised immigrants. In a 6–3 ruling on June 30, the Supreme Court struck it down, with Chief Justice John Roberts writing that children born to parents "unlawfully or temporarily present" are nonetheless "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States and are citizens at birth under the Fourteenth Amendment. Roberts's opinion did carve out the categories courts have long recognised as exceptions: children of accredited diplomats, of hostile occupying forces, and those born aboard foreign sovereign vessels or in a handful of outlying territories.

Thursday's orders are built almost entirely inside those carve-outs. Unlike the 2025 order, they do not touch the children of H-1B holders, international students or undocumented immigrants generally — the categories that drove most of the anxiety, and most of the litigation, the first time around. Instead the administration is wagering that a much narrower order, hewing closely to exceptions the Court itself just endorsed, can survive where the broad version could not.

## The legal fight resets, not ends

Civil rights groups are not conceding the point. Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU's Immigrants' Rights Project, said any renewed attempt to "rewrite" birthright citizenship "will meet the same fate as the last one," and lawyers involved in *Trump v. Barbara* — the case that produced June's ruling — are preparing new filings. The dispute this time is narrower but not trivial: whether "large categories of people who lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments," as Miller put it, can be read into an exception the Court intended for accredited diplomats with formal immunity, and whether denying entry to pregnant travellers on suspicion of birth-tourism intent — rather than after any fraud is established — survives due-process scrutiny. Immigration attorneys note the order's own list of exclusions is labelled "non-exhaustive," leaving room for the administration to expand it through agency guidance rather than further executive orders, which could itself become a point of legal attack.

![Jacob M. Howard, the Michigan senator who authored the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause in 1866, at the center of the current legal dispute.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Jacob_M._Howard_-_Brady-Handy.jpg/250px-Jacob_M._Howard_-_Brady-Handy.jpg)

## An industry braces for ambiguity, again

Birth tourism itself is a small and specific business — clusters of consultancies in Los Angeles and Miami and Chinese-, Russian- and Taiwanese-run "maternity hotels" charging $20,000 to $85,000 for packages that include a US birth certificate, according to immigration researchers who have tracked the practice for a decade. It is not the scale of that industry that concerns immigration lawyers and employers now, but the compliance fog the order creates around it. Consular officers will face pressure to question any visa applicant of childbearing age about pregnancy status and travel intent, a practice immigration firms warn is difficult to apply consistently and easy to challenge as discriminatory. Employers sponsoring foreign workers, universities enrolling international students, and hospitals accustomed to treating visiting patients are all bracing for slower, more unpredictable visa processing — even though none of those groups is a direct target of the new order.

That is the pattern immigration-dependent sectors have now lived through twice in seven months: an order, an injunction fight, a Supreme Court reckoning, and a redrafted order that starts the clock again. Each round adds friction — to consular wait times, to relocation planning, to the confidence with which a hospital, a university or a tech employer can tell a foreign hire what their child's legal status will be. None of it depends on the order ultimately being upheld; the uncertainty itself is the cost, and it resets every time Washington tries again.

## What's next

Civil rights groups are expected to file suit within days, most likely in the same federal courts that heard the original *Barbara* litigation, seeking a preliminary injunction before the 30-day agency guidance deadline lapses in early September. Whether a judge treats this order as meaningfully distinct from its predecessor — narrow enough to fit inside the Fourteenth Amendment exceptions the Supreme Court just reaffirmed — will be the first test of how much room, if any, that June ruling actually left the administration to manoeuvre.

sandisk-wd-skhynix-flash-slide.headline: SanDisk, Western Digital shares slide as SK Hynix flash memory outlook disappoints
sandisk-wd-skhynix-flash-slide.body_md:
Memory-chip stocks had their roughest week of the year, and the trigger came from an unlikely place: better-than-expected earnings.

SanDisk and Western Digital both beat Wall Street's profit targets when they reported quarterly results on Wednesday. Then their shares got hammered anyway — Western Digital sank as much as 16%, SanDisk fell 11%, and Micron dropped 6% in sympathy. The reason: guidance for the current quarter fell just short of the sky-high numbers investors had priced in, and after a year of parabolic gains, "just short" was enough to trigger a rout.

"The selloff looks absurd," Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi wrote of the reaction, noting both companies had actually delivered solid results. SanDisk guided to first-quarter revenue of $10.3 billion to $10.8 billion — a midpoint of roughly $10.55 billion against a consensus near $10.6 billion — and EPS of about $45, below whisper numbers that had crept as high as $50. That was the whole story: a slight miss against expectations inflated by a stock that was up 469% to 574% this year. Western Digital, up over 200% year-to-date, got caught in the same downdraft.

![A macro shot of a SanDisk NAND flash memory chip](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/31/SanDisk_SDSA4AH-032G_-_NAND_flash_SDTNNMCHSM-016G-0654.jpg)

## SK Hynix set the tone first

The ground had already shifted. SK Hynix, the South Korean giant that dominates both high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators and a large share of NAND flash production, reported record quarterly revenue of 79.3 trillion won (about $55 billion) in late July — and still saw its stock drop more than 9%, because analysts had modeled in even more. HBM4 shipments came in below forecast, pushing some revenue into later quarters, and the company guided that combined DRAM and NAND flash shipments would decline 10% to 20% next quarter from this one.

That shipment guidance was a flash memory-specific warning sign sitting in the middle of an otherwise triumphant earnings report, and it planted the first seed of doubt about how much further the AI-driven memory rally could run. When SK Hynix's own US-listed shares fell again this week — down more than 6% at one point — traders were reacting as much to the SanDisk and Western Digital guidance as to any fresh news of their own, plus a bout of thin-liquidity volatility on South Korea's new premarket trading venue that has made the stock swing wildly on almost no volume.

## A pricing problem, not (yet) a demand collapse

Underneath the guidance numbers is a more specific worry: how much of the memory boom is volume and how much is just price. SanDisk disclosed that roughly $2 billion of its sequential revenue growth came from pricing rather than shipments — a sign that NAND suppliers have been raising prices aggressively to capture AI-driven scarcity, not necessarily selling more chips. If pricing growth cools even slightly, as SK Hynix's shipment-decline guidance implies it might, margins that have looked spectacular this year become much harder to repeat.

SK Hynix's NAND arm, Solidigm, is meanwhile pushing ahead with a pre-IPO fundraising of up to $7 billion ahead of an expected Nasdaq listing at a valuation near $36 billion — a bet that investor appetite for flash memory exposure remains strong even as the near-term numbers wobble.

## What to watch

Micron reports its own quarterly results later this month, and its shipment and pricing commentary will be the next real test of whether this week's slide is profit-taking after an extraordinary run or the first sign that the memory supercycle is cresting. Until then, the sector's whipsaw trading says more about stretched expectations than about underlying chip demand.

clacton-by-election-record-field.headline: Farage faces record 34 candidates in Clacton by-election as Count Binface polls second
clacton-by-election-record-field.body_md:
The by-election was never really about who might win it. Nigel Farage will win it — polling from Survation in early August put him at 73 per cent, with the seat's main challenger a man in a bin costume trailing on 20. What the 13 August vote in Clacton will be remembered for is its ballot paper: 34 names long, printed on a sheet roughly 90 centimetres across, the largest field ever to contest a UK parliamentary seat.

The previous record, 26 candidates in the 2008 Haltemprice and Howden by-election, stood for eighteen years. Clacton beat it by eight.

## A resignation designed to be undone

Farage triggered the contest himself. He quit as MP for Clacton on 7 July, in the middle of a Parliamentary Standards Commissioner inquiry into whether he failed to declare a £5 million gift from the crypto financier Christopher Harborne, and a separate Sunday Times report alleging undeclared benefits — staff, security, housing — from George Cottrell, a Reform aide who served eight months in a US prison in 2017 after pleading guilty to wire fraud. The Sunday Guardian Live reported the National Crime Agency had also flagged the Harborne payment under anti-money-laundering rules.

Rather than face the inquiry, Farage resigned and stood again, framing it as a referendum on himself. "The voters of Clacton should be the judges," he said, casting the parliamentary standards process as a political weapon. It's a manoeuvre with precedent — MPs have long used by-elections to seek a fresh mandate mid-scandal — but rarely this openly telegraphed as a strategy to sidestep an ongoing probe rather than answer it.

![Count Binface, the satirical candidate polling second in the Clacton by-election](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0d/Count_Binface.jpg)

## Labour, the Tories and the Lib Dems all sat it out

What turned a routine by-election into a record-breaker was who didn't show up. Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Greens and Restore Britain all declined to field candidates, treating the contest as Farage's personal errand rather than a genuine electoral test. That left the field to Reform UK, minor parties and a long tail of independents — and, crucially, cleared space for a novelty run to become the de facto opposition.

Enter Count Binface: an "intergalactic space warlord" played by the comedian Jon Harvey, a veteran protest candidate who has previously stood against Boris Johnson in Uxbridge and for London mayor. His 20-point manifesto — filling potholes with copies of the 2024 Labour manifesto, relocating Parliament to a new "Bin HQ" in Weeley, sending Clacton to host Eurovision 2028 — is a joke, but the backing behind it isn't entirely. He has drawn grassroots donations and a public endorsement from the green-energy entrepreneur Dale Vince, and describes himself, straight-facedly, as a "unity candidate" for voters with nowhere else to put a protest vote. Laurence Fox is also on the ballot for the Reclaim Party, one of dozens of smaller names competing for a distant third.

## What the record actually measures

A 73-point lead is not a competitive race by any definition, and nobody seriously expects Farage to lose the seat he built Reform UK's national profile around. What the 34-candidate field measures instead is the absence of a credible mainstream alternative in a seat the big parties decided wasn't worth contesting, paired with a public appetite — visible in Binface's second-place polling — to register dissent through parody rather than through any of Westminster's actual opposition parties. It says more about the state of the opposition than about Farage's standing, which the finances questions have so far done little to dent.

The count itself, on the night of 13 August, will double as an unusually literal test of how long Britain's largest-ever ballot paper takes to process by hand.

fa-withdraws-infantino-support.headline: FA withdraws support for Fifa's Infantino as Uefa boycott threat persists
fa-withdraws-infantino-support.body_md:
England's Football Association has told Gianni Infantino it no longer backs his bid for a fifth term as Fifa president — the clearest sign yet that the row over his abandoned plan to sell off pieces of the World Cup has curdled into something more personal, and more dangerous to his hold on the job.

The FA's letter, sent this week, retracts an earlier endorsement and calls for "a full and robust review of Fifa's leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently, for the benefit of all 211 member nations and with the long-term stewardship of football at its heart." It joins Wales, Sweden and Serbia, whose federations withdrew support on Monday. None of them have to make good on that threat for months yet — the next Fifa presidential election isn't until March 2027, in Rabat — but the direction of travel matters more than the date.

![Gianni Infantino, president of Fifa](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e5/Gianni_Infantino_%282020%29.jpg)

## The plan that started it

The trigger was a proposal, unveiled in late July, to raise $4.2bn by selling roughly 20% of a new subsidiary called Fifa Forward Enterprise — the commercial engine that would have run World Cup broadcasting, sponsorship, ticketing and hospitality — at a valuation of about $20bn. The anchor investor was reported to be Thrive Eternal, a vehicle launched by Joshua Kushner, brother of Jared Kushner. For a body that markets itself as a not-for-profit steward of the world's game, selling a fifth of its crown jewel to a fund with White House family ties was always going to invite scrutiny.

It invited more than that. Uefa's 55 member associations voted to boycott Fifa competitions if the sale went ahead, calling it a case where "some things are simply too important to sell." Concacaf and the Asian confederation raised objections of their own, and inside Fifa two senior figures pushed back publicly — one resigned as a presidential adviser, another said staff had been misled about the scheme. Infantino scrapped it on 1 August, announcing the climbdown from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.

## Scrapping the plan wasn't enough

What happened next is the more interesting story. Uefa didn't stand down. It said it had "lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's presidency" and would keep its boycott in place — covering the Under-20 Women's World Cup in Poland this September, the Under-17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, the men's Under-17 tournament in Qatar, the Women's Champions Cup in Miami, and, most consequentially, the Women's World Cup in Brazil in mid-2027 — unless Fifa gives binding assurances that nothing like the stake sale is attempted again.

Infantino tried to draw a line under it at a crisis meeting in Rabat on 5 August, where Fifa's management board and secretary-general Mattias Grafström reaffirmed their backing and the organisation apologised in a letter to member associations, acknowledging "mistakes" and conceding the "process should have been handled differently." It didn't land. Uefa confirmed the following day that its position "holds." Former Portugal captain Luis Figo went further in a newspaper column, calling Infantino's conduct "the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed" and writing simply: "Infantino must go."

## Why the cohesion matters more than the proposal

The stake sale itself is dead. What's still live is whether Fifa's six confederations can be made to pull in the same direction, and that's the part with real money attached. The World Cup is Fifa's only genuinely global, quadrennial cash event — broadcast deals, sponsorship packages and betting markets are all priced on the assumption that the tournament happens on schedule with full participation. A Uefa boycott of lesser tournaments is an inconvenience; a Uefa boycott of the 2027 Women's World Cup, involving the confederation that supplies the bulk of the sport's commercial value, would be a different order of problem, and one that starts to look like fragmentation rather than a governance dispute.

Infantino, for now, has the votes that count inside Fifa's own structures. What he's losing is the assumption that his re-election is a formality. An emergency congress can be called if 20% of the 211 member associations request one, opening a path to a no-confidence vote — a low bar in percentage terms, a high one in practice, given how many federations still depend on Fifa's development funding. The FA's letter doesn't force that vote. It removes one more reason not to hold it.

The next marker is whether other major federations — Germany, France, Italy, Spain among them — follow England and Wales before Uefa's full membership meets again, and whether Fifa offers the written guarantees Uefa says it wants ahead of the September Under-20 Women's tournament in Poland, the first event actually at risk from the boycott.

green-party-membership-surge.headline: Green Party membership surge threatens to overtake Labour's
green-party-membership-surge.body_md:
There is a specific, slightly absurd number that Green Party organisers have taken to repeating: a new member roughly every ten minutes for the past eleven months. Multiply that out and it explains how a party that stood at around 66,000 members last September now claims 225,000 — while Labour, the party that has governed Britain since July 2024, has been losing members at almost exactly the same clip in reverse.

The Greens' growth tracks neatly to the arrival of Zack Polanski as leader. Elected in a landslide in September 2025 on an explicitly "eco-populist" platform — his words, borrowed as much from movement politics as from Westminster — Polanski said the party needed to "connect with that anger and turn it to hope, turn it to possible solutions" rather than keep talking, as he put it, in "stats and spreadsheets." Membership passed 100,000 within a month of his election. It crossed 200,000 in early March 2026, days after Hannah Spencer won the Gorton and Denton by-election — the Greens' first-ever Westminster by-election victory and their fifth MP — with the party adding more than 2,000 members a day in the fortnight that followed. A YouGov poll for Sky News taken around the same time put the Greens on 21%, ahead of a Labour and Conservative party tied on 16% apiece.

Labour's numbers, by contrast, have been sliding since Sir Keir Starmer took the leadership in April 2020, when the party still counted 532,046 members. The Electoral Commission's most recent annual return, published this week, put Labour's membership at the end of 2025 at 264,754 — its lowest in a decade, and a drop of 68,481, or roughly a fifth, in a single year. Donation income fell even harder, from £39.4 million in 2024 to £6.5 million in 2025.

## Two different kinds of number

Worth noting: the Greens' 225,000 figure is the party's own live count, not an audited one. The Electoral Commission's official year-end 2025 tally for the Greens was 186,441 — still a huge jump on prior years, but short of what the party is claiming for mid-2026. Real-time counters tend to run ahead of regulatory filings, and parties have every incentive to publicise the bigger number. The comparison with Labour's 264,754 is therefore a little apples-to-oranges, though the trend lines — one rising steeply, one falling — are not in dispute.

What membership numbers do not straightforwardly translate into is seats. The Greens hold four English constituencies plus Gorton and Denton, against Labour's hundreds. Members pay dues, knock on doors and vote in internal contests; they do not, by themselves, win general elections. Still, a party swelling toward a quarter of a million members while the party of government sheds a fifth of its own in a year says something about where activist energy is currently pooling. The Greens' Autumn Conference, in Brighton in late September, will be the next moment to watch — the first big stage for Polanski to make the case that the surge is durable rather than a post-by-election spike.

snp-motorhome-writeoff.headline: SNP writes off Peter Murrell's £124,550 motorhome, still owes him £60,000
snp-motorhome-writeoff.body_md:
The motorhome is gone from the books, if not from memory. In its latest annual accounts, filed with the Electoral Commission this month, the SNP has quietly written off the £124,550 it once carried on its balance sheet for a luxury Niesmann + Bischoff Smove 7.4e — the campervan bought by former chief executive Peter Murrell in late 2020 and paid for entirely with party funds.

The vehicle had already been depreciating for years by the time it vanished from the accounts altogether. Valued at £100,790 on 1 January 2024, it was written down to £41,284 by that December, and now, in the 2025 statements, to nothing. The accounts state simply that "the vehicle did not belong to the party" — a bloodless line for a saga that ran from a pandemic-era purchase pitched as a campaigning tool, to a short drive from a dealer in Rosyth, Fife, to the Dunfermline home of Murrell's mother, where it sat until police seized it as part of Operation Branchform.

Murrell, the estranged husband of former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon, pleaded guilty on 25 May to embezzling more than £400,000 from the party over roughly twelve years, and was sentenced on 23 June to five years and three months in prison. Operation Branchform cleared both Sturgeon and the SNP's former treasurer, Colin Beattie, of wrongdoing. A proceeds-of-crime hearing to determine what, if anything, can be clawed back was scheduled for the weeks after sentencing.

## Still on the hook

What makes the accounts an odd read is the entry sitting a few lines away from the write-off: the SNP still owes Murrell £60,000, from a loan he made the party in 2021. There was never a formal loan agreement, the accounts note, no interest charged, and no repayment terms agreed — and the party says Murrell has not formally asked for the money back. Whether it will ever be repaid, or eventually written off too, is left open. The SNP has separately said it intends to pursue recovery of the embezzled funds in full and has no plans to pay Murrell anything.

The motorhome write-off itself was not announced with any fanfare; it surfaced as one line in a set of accounts otherwise built to tell a recovery story. The party reported a £509,903 surplus for 2025, a reversal from a roughly £400,000 deficit the year before, achieved largely by cutting staff from 26 to 19 and trimming the wage bill from £1.4 million to £978,538 after redundancies announced in December 2024. Treasurer Peter Grant credited "very difficult cost cutting decisions," and First Minister John Swinney described the party as being in a position of "formidable financial strength." Membership, meanwhile, has fallen to around 51,000, down from nearly 59,000 in 2024 and 64,000 the year before.

The party's own auditors were less upbeat, flagging that manual journal entries and transactions between related parties remained at what they termed "heightened risk of fraud" — a caveat that sits uneasily next to a set of accounts still working through the fallout of the last one.

The proceeds-of-crime process, which will determine how much of Murrell's embezzled money the SNP actually recovers, is the next point at which the numbers in these accounts could move again.

senate-muslim-brotherhood-hearing.headline: Senate Judiciary hearing on Muslim Brotherhood network boycotted by Democrats
senate-muslim-brotherhood-hearing.body_md:
Ted Cruz walked into Room 226 of the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Wednesday, looked down the dais, and found himself alone. Every Democratic member of the Senate Judiciary Committee's subcommittee on federal courts had stayed away from his hearing, titled — without much subtlety — "Hidden in Plain Sight: Confronting the Muslim Brotherhood Network in America." No other Republicans showed either. For roughly two hours, it was Cruz, three witnesses, and a lot of empty chairs.

> "The American people should ask themselves why not a single member of the minority decided that a hearing on terrorism was worth their time," Cruz said, calling the vacant seats "an embarrassment."

The boycott wasn't a last-minute snub. Five Democratic senators — Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Mazie Hirono of Hawaii, Alex Padilla of California and Peter Welch of Vermont — announced days beforehand that they'd skip it, calling the whole exercise a "political creepshow."

> "Scapegoating Muslims may be a Texas Republican strategist's idea of 'solid gold' to whip up their voters, but Democrats have no intention of indulging this political creepshow, particularly after the recent violence targeting places of faith," the senators said in a joint statement. "Our focus is the costs families face thanks to rampant, non-stop Trump corruption."

![Sen. Ted Cruz, who chaired the hearing as the sole senator present](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/95/Ted_Cruz_official_116th_portrait.jpg)

## A hearing with a name attached

What gave the standoff its edge was timing. The hearing landed a day after Abdul El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit health director, won Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Cruz used his opening statement to draw a line from El-Sayed to the network he says his subcommittee was investigating, noting that El-Sayed's father-in-law, Jukaku Tayeb, has held leadership roles at CAIR-Michigan and other groups Cruz's witnesses linked to Brotherhood-affiliated organizing. One of those witnesses, Kyle Shideler of the Center for Security Policy, testified at length about Tayeb's history. The other two — Lara Burns, a former FBI special agent now at George Washington University's Program on Extremism, and Arielle Klepach of the National Jewish Advocacy Center — largely stuck to the network's broader domestic footprint.

El-Sayed has dismissed the line of attack as a substitute for engaging his policy platform. Democrats, for their part, framed the whole hearing as an attempt to import that same argument into a congressional record with the imprimatur of a Senate committee behind it.

## The backdrop: designations already in motion

The hearing didn't emerge from nowhere. In November 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing the State and Treasury departments to assess Muslim Brotherhood chapters for potential terrorist designation. By January, Washington had followed through, designating the Egyptian, Lebanese and Jordanian branches as specially designated global terrorists and imposing sanctions. Cruz's hearing was pitched as building the public case for scrutinizing the network's reach inside the United States — a domestic complement to those overseas designations. Critics counter that no such domestic organization has been designated, and that the hearing conflated foreign branches with American Muslim civic groups.

## What the empty seats signal

Congressional oversight hearings work, in theory, because both parties show up and contest the record — even adversarially. A hearing conducted by one senator, with witnesses chosen by that senator alone, produces a transcript but not much scrutiny. That's the Democrats' bet: better to deny the hearing legitimacy than to lend it a foil. It's also a gamble, since an empty dais lets Cruz's framing stand unchallenged in the official record, which is precisely why he made a point of narrating the absences on camera.

Whatever the merits of either side's read, the episode says more about the state of congressional oversight than about the Muslim Brotherhood itself. A subcommittee built for shared fact-finding on terrorism policy is instead functioning as a one-party stage — mirrored, not coincidentally, by a Senate floor increasingly organized around competing messaging operations rather than joint inquiry. The next test of whether that dynamic holds arrives with El-Sayed's general election campaign, where the Brotherhood allegation is likely to resurface as a live campaign issue rather than a hearing-room talking point.

nyc-hate-crime-data.headline: NYC hate crime data show anti-Jewish incidents made up 57% of 2026 total
nyc-hate-crime-data.body_md:
New figures released by the New York Police Department this week show that anti-Jewish incidents accounted for 56.9% of all confirmed hate crimes in the city during the first seven months of 2026 — a share so lopsided that the group with the next-highest count, victims targeted over sexual orientation, trailed by nearly six to one.

The numbers: 205 confirmed anti-Jewish hate crimes from January through July, against 34 tied to sexual orientation and a comparatively small tail of other bias categories. Jewish New Yorkers make up roughly 10% of the city's population of 8.3 million. Confirmed hate crimes citywide rose 9.4%, from 329 incidents in the same period last year to 360 this year — meaning almost the entire year-over-year increase in hate crime is attributable to incidents targeting Jews.

![NYPD vehicle in Manhattan](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c4/NYPD_%286058705565%29.jpg)

## The July spike

The month of July alone did much of the damage to the annual figures. Of 33 confirmed hate crimes citywide that month, 23 were classified as antisemitic — up 53% from the 15 recorded in July 2025. NYPD data show that works out to roughly one confirmed antisemitic hate crime every 25 hours across the seven-month window.

July also produced the incident that crystallized the numbers into a political flashpoint. On July 23, a 51-year-old man, Raul Morales, allegedly stabbed a 57-year-old man near Central Park West before walking several blocks to an Orthodox synagogue on West 86th Street and stabbing a 50-year-old Jewish man with a screwdriver as he stepped outside. Witnesses said the suspect shouted "Allahu Akbar" and "Justice for Islam" during the attacks. He was charged with attempted murder and assault as hate crimes and is being held without bail.

## A mayor under scrutiny

The data landed a little over seven months into Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration, and Jewish community leaders were quick to draw a line between the two. At a press conference on the Upper West Side the day after the stabbing, several elected officials and rabbis pressed the mayor to speak more forcefully against antisemitism; some accused him of tolerating rhetoric, tied to his past criticism of Israeli policy, that they say has emboldened attackers. Mamdani called the stabbings "hateful and despicable" and said afterward that antisemitism "will never be tolerated and will never be accepted" in the city, while rejecting the broader allegation that his own language contributed to the trend. City Hall has also noted, accurately, that overall violent crime — murders and shootings in particular — is running at or near historic lows for the same period.

## What the numbers don't settle

NYPD hate crime statistics count only incidents the department has classified and confirmed, a process that lags initial complaints and can shift as investigations close — a caveat researchers at groups such as the Nexus Project have raised when comparing year-to-year totals. The figures also don't distinguish motive with much granularity: an attack tied to reaction against Israeli military action in Gaza and one rooted in older forms of antisemitism land in the same bucket. What the data do establish cleanly is scale and trend — a rising count, concentrated overwhelmingly on one community, in a city where confirmed hate crime overall is also climbing.

The next data point arrives when the NYPD publishes its August hate crime tally, typically in the first half of the following month, which will show whether the July spike was an aftershock of the stabbing case or the start of a steeper climb.

antarctica-midwinter-rescue.headline: Australian aviation crew carries out daring midwinter Antarctica rescue
antarctica-midwinter-rescue.body_md:
The plane that flew the mission does not normally do this. The Australian Antarctic Division's leased Airbus A319 spends its working life shuttling scientists and cargo between Hobart and Wilkins Aerodrome during the Antarctic summer, when there is at least some daylight to land by. In the early hours of Friday, 31 July, it took off in winter darkness instead, bound for McMurdo Station on the other side of the continent, to bring home an American researcher who needed medical care no Antarctic base can provide.

Five hours later it touched down at McMurdo in complete darkness, with the temperature at −43°C and falling. A ground crew — facing the same cold, plus a stiff wind — had spent hours grading and compacting the station's snow runway to keep it usable as conditions worsened. Onboard were specialists from the AAD and the Centre for Antarctic, Remote and Maritime Medicine, sent at the request of the US Antarctic Program. The crew transferred the patient, refuelled, and flew on to Christchurch, where the patient is now receiving treatment.

![A Skytraders A319, the aircraft type used in the Antarctic evacuation, on the ice runway at McMurdo Station.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/49/Antarctica_McMurdo_Ice_Runway_Skytraders_A319.jpg)

"Every Antarctic mission demands absolute precision, but winter operations raise the complexity significantly," said Captain Al Wallach, who piloted the flight. "The conditions we encountered were right on the edge of even the most specialised aircraft capability." Asked about the patient, he kept it simple: "Our thoughts remain with the patient, and we wish them a full recovery."

## Nothing about this can be scheduled

What made the flight remarkable wasn't the distance — Hobart to McMurdo and back is well within the A319's 5,000-nautical-mile range — but the fact that almost everything about it had to be decided in real time. There is no instrument approach that accounts for a snow runway going soft in a rising wind, no dispatch system that reroutes around six hours of grading work that either finishes in time or doesn't. Weather forecasters, runway crews, flight planners and medical staff were reading conditions and adjusting the plan continuously, with no fallback airfield within reach once the aircraft passed a certain point south.

Emma Campbell, the AAD's head of division, called it "a complex operation carried out in the depths of the Antarctic winter" that "highlights both the capability of our people and the strong partnerships that underpin Antarctic programs around the world." It is not the first time the same aircraft has done something like this: it flew a similar winter evacuation from McMurdo in 2020, in milder −30°C conditions, on that occasion prompting the AAD's then general manager to credit "the great spirit of cooperation between Antarctic nations."

Midwinter medevacs from Antarctica remain rare by design — bases are provisioned and staffed each year on the assumption that nobody is getting out until spring. When the exception is unavoidable, the response still comes down to trained people making judgment calls in the dark, not a system executing a plan. The patient's recovery in Christchurch is the next thing to watch; the flight itself will be filed away as one more entry in a short, closely studied list of missions attempted only when there is no other option.

offshore-wind-freeze-lifted.headline: US court lifts Trump administration's freeze on offshore wind projects
offshore-wind-freeze-lifted.body_md:
A federal appeals court has formally closed the book on one of the Trump administration's earliest attempts to choke off offshore wind development, dismissing its appeal against a ruling that struck down a nationwide freeze on wind permitting. The result, now final, is that federal agencies must keep processing the approvals offshore wind developers need to build — the opposite of what the White House tried to order eighteen months ago.

The freeze dates to January 20, 2025, when President Trump signed a memorandum halting federal approvals for wind projects, onshore and offshore alike, pending a review of leasing and permitting practices. A coalition of eighteen state attorneys general, led by Massachusetts' Andrea Joy Campbell, sued that May, arguing the indefinite pause exceeded the administration's authority and put billions of dollars in committed investment at risk. In December 2025, a judge on the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts agreed, vacating the freeze as arbitrary, capricious and contrary to law. The administration appealed to the First Circuit in February — then quietly walked away from that appeal, which the court dismissed in mid-June.

![Offshore wind turbines at the Kentish Flats wind farm in the Thames Estuary, UK](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c0/Off-shore_Wind_Farm_Turbine.jpg)

## A losing streak in court

The permitting-freeze case was only the broadest of the administration's defeats. Separately, the Interior Department issued stop-work orders in December 2025 on five offshore projects under construction — Revolution Wind, Vineyard Wind 1, Empire Wind, Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind and Ørsted's Sunrise Wind — citing undisclosed national-security concerns. Judges in Washington were not persuaded. Royce Lamberth called the Revolution Wind order "the height of arbitrary and capricious action" in a January 12 ruling, and by early February all five projects had preliminary injunctions allowing work to resume. The government did not appeal any of them before the deadline lapsed.

## The pivot: buying projects out instead

Having lost the legal fight to block permits outright, the administration switched tactics: paying developers to abandon their federal leases voluntarily. On Wednesday, RWE agreed to relinquish leases off New York, California and Louisiana — roughly 7 gigawatts of potential capacity, enough to power more than five million homes — for $1.22 billion. RWE said it saw "no path forward to permit the projects for the foreseeable future" and is redirecting the money toward a Louisiana gas-export project and gas turbines elsewhere. That deal pushes total federal spending on offshore wind lease buybacks to nearly $4 billion, following earlier settlements with TotalEnergies, Invenergy, and the developers behind Golden State Wind and Bluepoint Wind.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum framed the buybacks as a return to "common sense" energy policy. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse called it something closer to bribery — taxpayer money used to kill projects the administration couldn't stop by decree. Both readings point to the same underlying fact: courts have consistently found the administration's regulatory shortcuts unlawful, forcing it to achieve the same end through negotiated, and costlier, means. A parallel case shows the pattern holding — on Thursday, a federal judge in Oregon ordered the Pentagon to resume stalled reviews of onshore wind farms, finding it had blown past statutory deadlines under a separate freeze imposed in the name of radar interference.

## What's next

With the appeals track exhausted, the fight over offshore wind's future now runs through Interior's checkbook rather than the courts — and through state capitals, where officials who won this case are already signaling more litigation if new lease buyouts or permitting delays surface. The next marker to watch is whether other developers follow RWE's lead and cash out rather than wait on permits the government has shown little appetite to issue.
